Frasers Property profit rises 23.5% in fiscal 2026
article:
Real estate investor, developer and operator Frasers Property has announced that its attributable profit grew by 23.5% y-o-y to $300.1 million for the full year ended Sept 30, 2026.

Higher contributions from Singapore retail, residential projects, industrial estate and land sales boosted profit before interest and tax (PBIT) by 10.6% y-o-y to $1.3 billion. Of this, about 82% was recurring income.

Net fair-value gains were “significantly higher” than the previous financial year, said the Singapore-listed group in a bourse filing on Nov 13 after market close.

This reflected the valuation uplift from redevelopment plans for the Valley Point site on River Valley Road, as well as gains from the divestments of completed retail assets in Australia.

Frasers Property and Mitsubishi Estate are jointly redeveloping the prime waterfront site with Valley Point Shopping Centre and Fraser Suites Singapore, into a residential, retail and serviced residence project .

During the year, the group released some $4.1 billion of capital, deploying it into higher-return projects and helping to reduce its net debt-to-total-equity ratio from 89.2% to 77.3%.

The capital released came from primarily stabilised assets. It included the restructuring of the hospitality portfolio , with Frasers Property divesting properties valued at around $1.1 billion in total while retaining the management income stream.

The group also sold about $500 million worth of industrial and logistics properties to Frasers Logistics & Commercial Trust (FLCT) and Frasers Property Thailand Industrial Freehold & Leasehold Reit (FTReit).

Part of the capital released went into higher-return projects including asset repositioning and strategic investments, which comprise the tender award of The Centrepoint ’s leasehold plot, acquisition of Cuppage Terrace, full ownership of Fraser Suites Singapore at Valley Point, and the redevelopment of Yishun 10 into a mixed-use complex with residential and retail spaces.

Frasers Property also replenished its residential land bank selectively in Singapore, Australia and China.

For instance, it secured government land sale sites at Bayshore Drive and Kallang Close in Singapore, expanded its pipeline in key growth corridors in Australia, and added two premium residential projects in Shanghai, through joint ventures.

Residential development continues to be a driver of cashflow and higher returns for Frasers Property, with around S$1.1 billion of unrecognised revenue as at Sept 30, 2026.

At the same time, the group advanced its build-to-core strategy in industrial and logistics. It delivered some 368,000 sq m (3.96 million sq ft) of gross floor area across markets and progressed an active multi-market development pipeline totalling about 874,000 sq m of gross floor area.

Group CEO Panote Sirivadhanabhakdi described FY2026 as “a year of disciplined execution”.

“We delivered stronger operating and financial performance, while actively reshaping the portfolio through capital recycling, partnerships and selective investments,” he added.

The group’s balance sheet has about $17.7 billion of non-Reit property assets remaining, according to the Nov 13 announcement.

This means there are still “multiple, flexible pathways” to create and realise value in the future, such as through redevelopment, repositioning and capital recycling, it stated.

Frasers Property’s business units also made leadership and organisational changes during the year.

They include Tony Lombardo’s appointment as group COO, Tan Wee Hsien as Singapore CEO , and Jai Mirpuri as the incoming CEO of Frasers Property Industrial from Jan 11, 2027.

Its hospitality business has become two specialised platforms — reestablishing Frasers Hospitality as a dedicated lodging operations platform, while housing hospitality investment and asset management under the group investment arm.

At Frasers Hospitality, Eu Chin Fen will step down as CEO from Jan 1, 2027, while Chew Hang Song continues in his role as COO of the company and reports to Sirivadhanabhakdi.

Meanwhile, Frasers Hospitality’s Eric Gan will lead asset management under group investment, reporting to Lombardo.

Looking ahead, while navigating a complex operating environment, the group is focused on delivering its residential and industrial and logistics development pipelines, including the Valley Point and Yishun 10 redevelopments.

Currently, it will continue to execute on its asset management and capital-light management initiatives to drive recurring and fee income.

title: Ikea and City Energy partner to integrate gas appliances into home design service
article:
Ikea Singapore has partnered Life by City Energy, the home solutions arm of town gas provider City Energy, to incorporate gas appliances and installation planning into the furnishing retailer’s Home Design Service.

The collaboration allows homeowners to plan their kitchen cabinetry, appliance placement and gas piping requirements together before renovation begins.

Life by City Energy is the first partner to expand Ikea's Home Design Service, which was launched in 2025.

Under the arrangement, homeowners can select gas hobs, cooker hoods, gas water heaters and dryers from Life by City Energy as part of their home design plans.

An Ikea Home Design specialist will remain the homeowner's main point of contact, coordinating with Life by City Energy's specialists on appliance specifications, gas piping requirements and installation.

Once homeowners proceed with their design proposal, site visits and technical checks will be arranged where necessary. Ikea will handle cabinetry and appliance positioning, while Life by City Energy will arrange appliance delivery, installation and gas connections through its teams and partners.

Previously, homeowners using the Home Design Service had to source gas appliances separately and provide their specifications before kitchen plans could be finalised.

The partnership aims to reduce the need for separate arrangements and minimise potential installation delays or mismatched specifications.

“By bringing Life by City Energy solutions into that journey, customers can now bring their gas appliances and requirements into that conversation earlier, too, so more of the home can be planned together from the start,” said Steve Croasdale, commercial manager for Ikea Singapore, in a November 2026 press release

Soh Guan Hong, senior vice-president of residential sales at City Energy, said:  “With town gas infrastructure available in all new HDB flats, gas remains an integral part of Singapore's residential infrastructure, serving daily cooking, water heating and even laundry drying needs.”

The expanded Home Design Service is available at Ikea Alexandra and Ikea Tampines.

title: What's moving the market: Singapore's biggest property deals and hottest searches (Nov 13)
article:
Here is this week’s data-led look at Singapore’s property market, covering record transactions, rental benchmarks and the most searched homes on EdgeProp.

The following insights are compiled from EdgeProp Buddy , URA Realis and data.gov.sg, downloaded as of Nov 10.

Non-landed private homes — new launches, resales and rents

By transaction volume, Thomson Reserve saw the highest activity among new launch condos in the past fortnight to Nov 10, with 1,122 deals recorded.

The mega project, with over a thousand homes, debuted on Oct 31 with a take-up rate exceeding 90% at its VIP preview and launch day.

Lucerne Grand in Jurong West, Union Square Residences along Havelock Road, and Dunearn House on Dunearn Road were next on the list with 27, 24 and 21 transactions respectively.

All 10 of the most expensive condo units sold in the past fortnight also came from Thomson Reserve, involving homes on the highest floors.

Topping the list was a 30th-storey apartment fetching close to $5.98 million or $3,306 psf.

Following closely were a 29th-storey unit at nearly $5.96 million and a 28th-storey unit at around $5.94 million.

In the condo rental market, a unit at Meyerhouse in the Tanjong Katong area is being leased out for $21,500 per month, placing it among the highest rents in the Rest of Central Region (RCR) or city fringe.

Units at Riviere along Jiak Kim Street and Coastline Residences in the East Coast area also made the list with monthly rents of $18,000 and $14,000 respectively.

Landed homes — highest transacted prices and rents

In the Caldecott Hill Estate Good Class Bungalow (GCB) area, in District 11, a landed home along Olive Road was resold for $26.75 million. That works out to $1,467 psf based on its freehold land area of 18,241 sq ft.

Another GCB area yielded the next priciest deal in the landed property segment. A house on Oriole Crescent in the Raffles Park GCB area went for $24.5 million, or $2,411 psf on its freehold site area of 10,163 sq ft.

As for the leasing market in the RCR, the highest monthly rent achieved by a landed house was $31,000 or $4.96 psf. The detached house on Broadrick Road, off Mountbatten Road near the East Coast, measures around 6,250 sq ft.

Meanwhile, a terraced house along Race Course Road in Farrer Park is bringing in $27,000 a month, and a detached house on Jalan Kampong Chantek in Bukit Timah is fetching $20,000 a month.

HDB flats — top prices and rents, most transacted blocks

The public housing resale market saw a new islandwide record-high transaction price when a five-room flat in Dawson fetched $1.818 million on Oct 30. It is part of the SkyParc @ Dawson development, on the 40th to 42nd storeys.

The seller’s agent, Ted Wong of ERA, told EdgeProp Singapore that more than eight offers were received from prospective buyers.

The highest rents for HDB flats in the last 14 days stood at between $4,900 to $5,500 per month.

A three-room flat on Lim Liak Street in Bukit Merah took pole position, followed by a five-room flat along Clementi Avenue 3 with a $5,100 monthly rent.

As Singapore’s largest bank, DBS is a familiar blue-chip business with an established track record of both profitability and shareholder returns.
That record has held up even as interest rates fell.
DBS’s total income for the first nine months of 2026 (9M2026) rose 2% year on year (YoY) to a new high of S$17.9 billion, and net profit climbed 2% YoY to a record S$8.82 billion.
Total income for 3Q2026 slipped 1% YoY to S$5.85 billion and net profit fell 5% YoY to S$2.81 billion, mainly because of lower markets trading income.
Net interest income, the bank’s core lending earnings, still grew 4% YoY to S$3.71 billion.
The bank declared a 3Q2026 ordinary dividend of S$0.66 per share, plus a capital return dividend of S$0.15 per share.
Reinvesting the dividend can buy more shares, generating more payouts for your child in the future.
With DBS, parents can also easily introduce the
idea of owning
part of a real business to their child.
However, putting a large portion of your child’s money into a single stock, even one as strong as DBS Group, can be risky.
If anything happens to the bank or the banking sector in general, the investment could fall sharply in value.
Option #2: A Broad-Market ETF
With a broad-market exchange-traded fund (ETF), your child’s money enjoys diversification from the very first dollar.
For example,
Vanguard S&P 500 ETF
(NYSEARCA: VOO) tracks 500 large-cap U.S. companies, offering access to technology and scalable global sectors absent from the Singapore market.
With one investment, the money gains exposure to 500 companies, without parents analysing and attempting to pick the biggest winner.
With a broad-market ETF, poor performance from an individual company has less impact on the overall portfolio.
That said, returns will broadly follow the underlying market.
As at 31 October 2026, the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF has returned 11.76% year-to-date and an average 12.04% a year over the past five years.
In comparison, the share price of
Apple Inc (NASDAQ: AAPL)
, maker of the iPhone, rose by an average of about 18.1% a year over the same five years, and it is up around 26.8% so far in 2026.
By owning the whole market, investors give up the chance to significantly outperform it through a single standout stock.
When investing in ETFs, Singapore investors need to consider ETFs’ expense ratios, management fees, and any foreign exchange risk.
Option #3: A Singapore REIT
S-REITs turn your child’s savings into property income, without buying physical real estate.
A favourite amongst Singapore investors, S-REITs typically pay out at least 90% of their taxable income to enjoy tax transparency.
Defensive REITs like
CapitaLand Integrated Commercial Trust
(SGX: C38U), or CICT, generate steady cash flows through regular distributions, which can be reinvested to accelerate growth.
However, a REIT’s income is highly dependent on factors like occupancy levels, rental growth, and interest rates.
Gearing, interest costs and debt maturities can affect the distribution per unit (DPU) and its sustainability.
You might be in for a shock if you focus solely on headline yield without analysing the underlying business.
Why Time Changes the Answer
A five-year-old gives you a powerful 15- to 20-year runway for compounding growth.
Short-term market volatility matters less when the investment has decades to grow.
And with the long investment horizon, compounding becomes the true force.

And then, there is capital appreciation.

That’s a gain of about 274% before counting dividends or the bonus shares DBS has since issued to shareholders.
Do You Actually Have to Pick Just One?
Instead of an either-or choice, you can easily combine all three to minimise concentration risk while giving your child’s portfolio a chance to outperform the market.
With an initial investment of S$10,000, you can split it into:

Instead of 20 different stocks, keep it simple for your child’s portfolio.
This makes it easier to teach them what they own and why these investments are chosen.
The Most Important Investment May Not Be the Stock
Rather than focusing only on which stock is making money, show your child how you chose each investment, which companies they indirectly own and how payouts arrive.
Through this, you teach them ownership, not speculation.
This portfolio becomes an important financial education tool.
Your child can understand how underlying businesses earn, rather than focusing on daily share-price movements.
By the time they take over the portfolio, they will have a better understanding of investing and will not be going into the market blind.
Get Smart: Give Your Child Time and Ownership

A combination of all three can provide growth, income, and diversification.

title: Keppel vs Sembcorp: Which Stock Offers Better Value and Dividends Today?
article:
Keppel Ltd
(SGX: BN4) and
Sembcorp Industries
(SGX: U96) aren’t your typical old-school conglomerates anymore.
Keppel dropped its traditional heavy industries in favour of a leaner, asset-light approach, focusing on generating steady fees rather than tying up capital.
Sembcorp, on the other hand, made a decisive shift towards green energy, expanding rapidly in the renewables space.
With their valuations heading in different directions, which stock offers the better current yield and
long-term value
today?
Keppel: Can Its Asset-Light Transformation Unlock More Value?
Keppel has moved away from its roots as an offshore conglomerate, pushing hard to become a global player in asset management, infrastructure, and connectivity.
Expanding recurring management fees and operating cash flows provides far greater earnings predictability, with recurring income in the first nine months of 2026 (9M2026) growing over 10% year-on-year (YoY).
In 9M2026, asset management fees surged 18% to S$354 million as Keppel added about S$19.5 billion of new FUM year to date, while core net profit for “New Keppel” jumped over 20%.
Keppel has announced S$3.7 billion of asset monetisations so far in 2026, beating its S$2 billion to S$3 billion full-year target.
Completed deals have so far brought in about S$940 million in cash.
In sum, Keppel’s investment appeal increasingly depends on its ability to grow recurring earnings and unlock value from its existing assets.
Sembcorp Industries: Can Energy Growth Sustain Its Momentum?
Sembcorp Industries runs on a dual engine, blending steady cash flows from the conventional Gas and Related Services segment with aggressive renewables expansion across Singapore and international markets.
This strategy drove revenue in the first half of 2026 (1H2026) to S$3.771 billion, up 28% from a year ago. But underlying net profit was down 25% to S$369 million.
The Gas and Related Services segment anchored Sembcorp Industries’ results with S$285 million in segmental profit. The segment is backed by having 80% of Singapore’s contracted load locked in for five years or more.
Renewables earnings softened to S$69 million because of curtailment, tax changes, and resource headwinds in China.
Including Alinta Energy for the full half-year, underlying net profit would have been S$558 million on a pro forma basis, on S$5.589 billion in turnover.
With gross capacity at 35.4 gigawatts (GW) (21.9 GW in renewables) and an interim dividend up 22% to S$0.11 per share, Sembcorp is relying on Australian contributions and land sales for a stronger 2H2026.
For investors, Sembcorp offers a front-row seat to the region’s growing appetite for energy and rapid expansion of green infrastructure.
But keeping up this progress isn’t straightforward.
It faces unpredictable swings in merchant power prices, weather risks that can throw off projections, and the high costs that come with folding new acquisitions into its business.
Keppel vs Sembcorp: Which Has Stronger Financial Fundamentals?

On a reported basis, both companies’ profits fell sharply in 1H2026 because of one-off items: legacy-asset losses at Keppel and Alinta deal costs at Sembcorp.
Stripping these out, Keppel’s core business grew while Sembcorp’s underlying profit shrank.
Both generated healthy free cash flow, but debt has risen at both: Keppel’s net debt to EBITDA climbed to 6.7 times, while Sembcorp’s reached 5.3 times after its Alinta purchase.
Which Stock Offers Better Dividend Income?
Sembcorp Industries takes the immediate lead on yield.
At S$5.68 per share as of 6 November 2026, its S$0.22 annualised payout delivers a 3.87% dividend yield, giving income investors a clear head start over Keppel.
Keppel traded at S$9.45 as of 6 November 2026 with an annualised ordinary dividend of S$0.30 per share, translating to a 3.17% yield.
Beyond the headline numbers, Sembcorp’s payouts are plain cash dividends, whereas Keppel’s historical returns have periodically relied on special dividends or distributions in-specie (paying shareholders in
Keppel REIT
(SGX: K71U) units instead of cash).
When it comes to sustainability, both companies bring different strengths.
Sembcorp’s dividend coverage is backed by reliable cash flows from its gas division, where 80% of Singapore power load is locked into long-term contracts.
However, heavy capital expenditure (capex) for green buildouts and debt-funded acquisitions naturally limit aggressive dividend expansion.
Keppel’s asset-light model provides a stronger structural growth runway.
By monetising legacy assets, unlocking S$940 million in 2026 cash proceeds, and driving high-margin fund management fees, Keppel enjoys superior free cash conversion that can comfortably fund future payout growth.
Which Stock Offers Better Value at Today’s Share Price?
Valuations reflect two very different market stories.
Sembcorp trades at a price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 17.05x and a price-to-book (P/B) ratio of 1.91x, pricing it as a traditional, capital-intensive utility.
Keppel commands a steeper P/E ratio of 30.55x as the market re-rates it from a traditional conglomerate into a global asset manager.
Future returns for Keppel hinge on executing its asset-light pivot, scaling FUM past S$106 billion towards a
2030 target of S$200 billion
, while deploying its S$23 billion deal pipeline.
The main risk is paying a high P/E of 30.55x if global fundraising slows.
Sembcorp’s upside depends on integrating Alinta Energy, expanding renewables capacity to 25 GW by 2028, and maintaining strong power margins.
Its primary vulnerability stays tied to wholesale power price volatility and heavy capex demands.
Get Smart: Which Stock Deserves Your Money?
Choosing between these two
blue chips
pits an asset-light compounder against a utility’s steady cash flow.
When comparing their key deliverables, Sembcorp wins for immediate income with its higher dividend yield, while also offering a cheaper valuation multiple for a wider margin of safety.
But Keppel is built for the future. The company’s transformation into a global asset manager means it brings in high-margin fees and consistently strong returns on equity.
Plug into Sembcorp if you want immediate dividend income and solid value.
But for superior long-term total returns, Keppel is the overall champion, as its transformation into a global asset manager packs the ultimate structural power for your portfolio.

title: ST Engineering Share Price: Is This Defence Stock Still Worth Buying?
article:
Singapore Technologies Engineering
(SGX: S63), or ST Engineering, has
rallied strongly
over the past few years.
Rising defence budgets and the steady commercial aerospace sector explain much of the share price gain.
But after a staggering run like this, how much of the future is already reflected in the share price?
In this article, we evaluate whether today’s valuation is justified by the business, or if you can afford to wait for better opportunities.
ST Engineering: More Than Just a Defence Stock
ST Engineering has a nicely diversified business across three main segments: Commercial Aerospace (CA), Defence & Public Security (DPS), and Urban Solutions & Satcom (USS).
Its CA segment provides aftermarket maintenance, repair, and operations (MRO) services for, as you might guess, commercial aircrafts.
As Singapore’s prime defence major, ST Engineering also provides defence equipment, military systems and security solutions for governments and armed forces worldwide through its DPS segment.
Finally, USS covers smart city systems, transport technology and satellite communications.
Overall, these businesses provide different economic exposures and ensure ST Engineering does not solely rely on a particular industry.
Much of the work also runs on long contracts with governments and airlines, which make future revenue more predictable compared to other companies.
Why Is Driving ST Engineering’s Growth?
Defence spending is the
headline driver
.
Global military spending has risen over recent years, as countries increasingly look to upgrade their defence capabilities given the conflicts in Russia/Ukraine and the Middle East.
This trend, unlikely to slow anytime soon, plays into ST Engineering’s DPS segment, which has benefitted from more contracts for defence and military solutions.
Aircraft maintenance is the quieter one.
Like defence, global spending on MRO activities has picked up as global aircraft fleets age and require more maintenance and upkeep work.
This dual engine has resulted in a steadily increasing order book for ST Engineering.
As of 30 June 2026 (1H2026), the order book hit a record S$35.7 billion, up 14% from a year earlier, with S$5.7 billion due to be delivered in the rest of 2026.
Given the group’s FY2025 (ending 31 December 2025) total revenue of S$12.35 billion, the current order book provides close to three years of revenue visibility.
That said, a big order doesn’t automatically guarantee big profits.
Execution risk still matters, and higher costs could whittle down the margins of each contract, ultimately resulting in lower profits.
Are ST Engineering’s Earnings Keeping Up with Its Share Price?
So far, yes.
In 1H2026, revenue rose 11% to S$6.6 billion and net profit climbed 27% to S$512 million, so earnings are growing faster than sales.
CA led the way, with operating profit up 29%. DPS grew 10%, and USS almost quadrupled its operating profit (albeit from a low base) after cost cuts.
Cash is coming in too.
Operating cash flow rose 26% to S$960 million, and free cash flow improved to S$591.6 million from S$591.6 million from S$484.6 million.
Meanwhile, debt looks manageable.
Borrowings were S$4.7 billion against S$255.3 million of cash and cash equivalents as of 30 June 2026, with the group steadily deleveraging across the past year.
Is ST Engineering’s Current Valuation Justified?
This is where it gets harder.
As at 12 November 2026, ST Engineering trades at trailing and forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratios of 57.1x and 26.1x, respectively.
Against their historical averages, these earnings ratios seem stretched.
The market is clearly paying up for defence exposure and earnings visibility.
If profit growth slows, the multiple could shrink, with the share price going nowhere even while the underlying business keeps doing well.
ST Engineering’s new dividend policy dictates a base dividend of S$0.18 per share for 2026 plus about a third of any rise in underlying profit per share.
Interim payments of S$0.04 and S$0.05 have been made so far.
Free cash flow of S$591.6 million in 1H2026 comfortably covered the S$468.2 million paid out in dividends during the half.
But at S$9.74 (as at 12 November 2026), the trailing yield is roughly 2.5%, which does not scream attractive to income investors.
What Could Drive ST Engineering’s Next Phase of Growth?
More defence contracts from an international pipeline, additional aircraft maintenance capacity and increasing profit contribution from USS could help.
Continued conversion of order backlogs to underlying profits and cash flows, alongside any improvements in operating margins, will be beneficial for ST Engineering as well.
The key risks for the group include delays or cost overruns on big projects, weaker margins and slower contract wins.
Already, new orders in 1H2026 were S$7.6 billion, down from S$9.1 billion a year earlier.
Get Smart: A Strong Business, but Is the Price Right?
Undoubtedly, ST Engineering is a well-diversified group that benefits from strong spending in
global defence
and commercial aerospace.
A S$35.7 billion order book provides good revenue visibility moving forward, but execution risk could still present a possible concern for future profit and cash generation.
However, the current price already reflects most of that.
Current valuations leave little room for disappointment.
Long-term investors who like the business would do better waiting for a more reasonable valuation, or building a position gradually over time.

title: 3 SGX Next 50 Stocks More than Doubling the STI’s Return YTD
article:
The Straits Times Index lost ground in October, but the dip barely dented a good year.
The
SPDR Straits Times Index ETF
(SGX: ES3), which tracks the
Straits Times Index
(SGX: ^STI), delivered a total return of 18.7% from the start of 2026 to the end of October.
Three SGX
Next 50
stocks did far better.
UMS Integration Limited
(SGX: 558) returned 77.4%.
Frencken Group Limited
(SGX: E28) and
Pan-United Corporation Ltd
(SGX: P52) followed with 43.0% and 40.3%.
These figures include
dividends
, and each one more than doubled the ETF’s gain.
So, did the businesses keep pace with their share prices? It depends on the company.
Is Singapore’s building pipeline showing up in Pan-United’s numbers?
Pan-United is Singapore’s largest ready-mix concrete supplier.
In the first half of 2026 (1H2026), revenue grew 37% year on year (YoY) to S$549.6 million as construction activity picked up across Singapore, Malaysia and Vietnam.
Singapore brought in S$485.9 million, or about 88% of group revenue.
Profit grew even faster.
Net profit attributable to shareholders rose 49% YoY to S$30.6 million.
Operating leverage helped, as did efficiencies from the group’s AiR Digital platform.
Pan-United raised its interim dividend by 50% to S$0.015 per share and paid it on 4 September 2026.
Free cash flow (FCF) improved to S$7.5 million from S$1.0 million a year ago as capital expenditure fell.
The group held S$86.2 million in cash against S$21.0 million in borrowings and S$39.5 million in lease liabilities.
Investors may also be looking ahead.
The Building and Construction Authority (BCA) expects S$47 billion to S$53 billion in construction demand for 2026, and S$31 billion of that had been awarded by June.
Changi Airport Terminal 5, the Marina Bay Sands expansion and MRT extensions anchor the pipeline.
On the flip side, FCF is still thin next to profit.
Trade receivables tied up S$26.0 million as sales grew.
Management also flagged energy costs and supply chain disruptions as risks.
How much of UMS’s profit growth came from its operations?
UMS makes precision parts and assembles equipment modules for
semiconductor
equipment makers.
In the third quarter of 2026 (3Q2026), revenue rose 61% YoY to S$95.4 million, while net profit attributable to shareholders more than doubled to S$21.1 million.
Semiconductor revenue grew 65% to S$83.1 million and aerospace revenue rose 55% to S$9.7 million, as component production ramped up for a new major customer.
Not all of it was good news.
Gross material margin narrowed to 52% from 58.2% because of product mix.
Profit also got a lift from a S$1.6 million foreign exchange gain, which came from currencies, not customers.
Cash flow is more reassuring.
FCF was S$14.9 million, against an outflow of S$10.8 million a year ago.
UMS ended September with S$49.0 million in cash and S$5.0 million in bank borrowings, before completing a S$138.6 million share placement in October.
The board proposed a third interim dividend of S$0.010 per share, payable on 18 December 2026.
With 177.6 million bonus shares issued in January and 52.9 million placement shares in October, that rate now applies to more shares.
What might investors be paying for?
Possibly what comes next.
UMS’s new major customer has issued upbeat guidance on AI-driven demand.
Industry association SEMI expects global spending on 300mm chip fabrication equipment to rise 31% to US$149 billion in 2026.
Why did Frencken’s shares rise when its profit fell?
Frencken builds complex electro-mechanical assemblies and plastic components for semiconductor, healthcare and automotive companies, among others.
At first glance, its 1H2026 results looked flat: revenue slipped 0.8% YoY to S$427.8 million and net profit attributable to shareholders fell 3.4% to S$19.3 million.
The detail looks better.
Gross margin widened by 0.9 percentage points to 15.0%, and gross profit grew 5.8% to S$64.4 million.
Administrative expenses rose 9.9% on staff and transformation costs.
Management expects 2H2026 revenue to beat both 2H2025 and 1H2026.
It guides for higher full-year revenue and profit, with semiconductor sales expected to rise.
To put it simply, investors may be paying for where Frencken is heading, not where it has been.
Cash flow is the part to watch.
FCF swung to an outflow of S$15.3 million from an inflow of S$50.6 million a year ago, as inventories and receivables absorbed S$81.6 million.
Frencken still holds S$68.8 million in net cash.
The missing interim dividend is normal, as Frencken pays dividends once a year with its full-year results.
FCF is the lifeblood of dividends, so second-half cash flow will shape the final payout.
Get Smart: Write down what the price expects
All three share one trait.
Their share prices appear to reflect where earnings could go, not just where they are today.
A simple habit helps here.
When a stock runs ahead of its results, write down what the business needs to deliver next.
For Frencken, that means a stronger second half and higher full-year profit.
For UMS, it means sales from its new major customer growing without margins slipping further.
Then check each set of results against your list, and you will know quickly whether the story still holds.

title: Lutnick under fire as Bessent blames Commerce Secretary in Nvidia crisis
article:
(Nov 13): Fallout from Jensen Huang’s ouster as Nvidia Corp chief executive officer is reaching deep into Washington, where Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is confronting accusations that his department didn’t do enough to keep the company’s prized artificial intelligence (AI) chips out of China’s hands.

As the ultimate overseer of US export control programmes, Lutnick is accountable for any policy or enforcement gaps that allowed Nvidia’s AI processors to reach unauthorised Chinese buyers. Internal tension over his role burst into the open on Friday when Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed him for failing to blacklist a Singapore-based company, Megaspeed, over possible violations.

“Treasury, USTR and State — they were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months but Commerce has the pen,” Bessent said in an interview with CNBC. “We have all the authorities that we need. They just need to be implemented.”

Lutnick is a controversial figure in President Donald Trump’s orbit. People with ties to the White House, who asked not to be identified describing private conversations, said he’s been marginalised within the administration for a while. At the same time, his exit has been predicted before, and he’s still in the job.

As of Thursday, the Commerce chief retained Trump’s blessing. In a statement, the White House said Trump maintains complete confidence in the secretary and his ability to carry out the position as the most transformative commerce secretary in modern history.

See also: Maga’s midterm defeat won’t change the course of history

Congress is now demanding answers from Lutnick and other Trump administration officials about decisions that may have made it easier for China to obtain Nvidia’s advanced chips as well as the degree to which Silicon Valley leaders like Jensen Huang may have influenced policy.

Pressure on the administration and the tech sector is escalating a week after an election where voters expressed intense frustrations over the impact of the AI boom.

Huang’s abrupt departure was prompted by revelations that he’d had an affair with a woman suspected by US officials of spying for China and Megaspeed had been under investigation by Commerce for possible export control violations. Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing, while the former Nvidia chief’s romantic partner, Alice Huang, is now in China.

See also: Musk drove the Cybertruck and Tesla’s EV ambitions off a cliff

“I would like for Secretary Lutnick ASAP to come testify before the Senate Banking Committee because we have a lot of bipartisan questions and concerns about what’s happened over the last year,” Senator Jim Banks, an Indiana Republican, said in an interview on Fox News.

Late on Thursday night, a Commerce Department spokesperson, Kristen Eichamer, said Lutnick has agreed to testify.

Axios reported on Wednesday that Trump had authorised a new crackdown on companies suspected of diverting advanced AI chips to China, but that Lutnick delayed acting on the directive. Representative Raja Krishnamoorthi, an Illinois Democrat, called the report “deeply, deeply disturbing”.

On at least three separate occasions earlier this year — in May, August and earlier this month — Trump approved taking action against suspected diversions of Nvidia chips to China, Axios reported.

This week’s events are “a freaking disaster at this point, and it deserves tremendous scrutiny not only by obviously Nvidia’s board, but by the intelligence community and the US government as well,” Krishnamoorthi said in an interview on Bloomberg Television on Wednesday.

Further complicating the dynamic are allegations by Democratic lawmakers that Lutnick’s sons, who hold leadership positions at Cantor Fitzgerald, are profiting off of policy decisions that he makes. Lutnick, who previously was CEO of Cantor, divested his stake as legally required before becoming secretary, and elevated his sons to top jobs at the firm.

The Commerce Department didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. Cantor Fitzgerald declined to comment.
